title: "All or Nothing" Exercise Exhausts the Soul
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This article from Stuart's depressurizing the teacher's soul series reframes exercise as a tool for self-depressurization rather than achievement or body-image optimization. Stuart argues that the 'all or nothing' mentality toward exercise — either a rigorous regimen or nothing at all — is counterproductive because it adds achievement pressure to what should be a release valve. He redefines exercise as simply 'using the body': standing instead of sitting, walking during prep, cycling instead of driving — low-bar activities that disrupt the Workload-Pressure Cycle without adding new pressure. Practical school-based suggestions include standing desks, hallway walks during prep time, and embedding incidental movement into the workday alongside Moments of Genuine Connection with colleagues. The article frames consistent, modest physical activity as a form of rebellion against burnout and an act of care for family, students, and self.
points: The 'all or nothing' mentality toward exercise defeats its purpose as a depressurizer — adding achievement pressure to a stress-relief practice cancels the benefit
Stuart redefines exercise as 'using the body,' setting a deliberately low bar that makes it sustainable and sustainable habits are what actually interrupt the Workload-Pressure Cycle
Exercise that produces a sweat has a similar effect on anxiety to a beer — minus the downsides — making it one of the most efficient internal pressure-release mechanisms available
School-based exercise strategies (standing desk, hallway walks, brief outdoor movement) embed depressurization into the existing workday without requiring extra time
Sustained, joyful physical activity reaffirms that teachers are embodied souls — an attitude that counters the disembodied, productivity-only culture of overwork
